procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 27.01.2020 of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M No.40507 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 1, aggrieved by the order of the Additional Sessions Judge, Nuh, approached the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.). The High Court allowed the petition on 27.01.2020, setting aside the order of the Additional Sessions Judge and ordering the summoning of the Appellants under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. as additional accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants, discontented with their summoning by the High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal and modified the impugned order of the High Court dated 27.01.2020.

directions: The impugned order of the High Court dated 27.01.2020 is modified.
The Trial Court shall follow the cited dictum and proceed against Appellant No. 1 in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is sufficient evidence against the Appellants to summon them as additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellants are the father-in-law (No. 1), sister-in-law (No. 2), and brother-in-law (No. 3) of a deceased woman.
An FIR for dowry-related offenses was filed against the appellants, the husband, and the mother-in-law.
Following an investigation, the police filed a chargesheet only against the husband and mother-in-law, finding no incriminating material against the appellants.
During the trial, the deceased's brother filed an application under Section 319 CrPC to summon the appellants as additional accused.
The Trial Court dismissed this application, but the High Court overturned that decision and ordered the summoning of all three appellants.
The appellants challenged the High Court's summoning order before the Supreme Court.
law: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 of the CrPC is an extraordinary power and should not be exercised routinely.
The standard of proof required is higher than a prima facie case; there must be credible evidence strongly indicating the person's involvement.
The evidence against the person to be summoned should carry a similar weight and value as the evidence against those already facing trial.
This power ought not to be invoked in the absence of credible evidence or based on mere strong suspicion.
application: The Supreme Court applied the legal standard to each appellant individually.

For Appellant No. 1 (the father-in-law), the Court found specific evidence on record that he had asked the deceased's brother to spend 20 lakhs on the marriage. This was deemed sufficient to meet the high threshold for summoning under Section 319 CrPC.
For Appellant Nos. 2 and 3 (the sister-in-law and brother-in-law), the Court found no credible evidence connecting them to the death of the deceased.
The Court determined that summoning Appellant Nos. 2 and 3 would be "farfetched" and based on "mere strong suspicion," which is insufficient to invoke the power under Section 319 CrPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court ruled partly in favor of the appellants. It held that there was sufficient evidence to summon the father-in-law (Appellant No. 1) as an additional accused. However, it found no credible evidence against the sister-in-law (Appellant No. 2) and brother-in-law (Appellant No. 3). Therefore, the Supreme Court upheld the summoning of Appellant No. 1 but set aside the High Court's order summoning Appellant Nos. 2 and 3.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is sufficient evidence against the Appellants to summon them as additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellants challenged the High Court's order summoning them as additional accused. Their argument aligns with the Trial Court's initial finding that the extraordinary power under Section 319 Cr.P.C. should only be exercised when evidence strongly indicates involvement. They contended that the deposition of Respondent No. 1 and other material on record were insufficient to establish that they had committed an offense for which they could be tried alongside the existing accused.
respondent_arguments: Respondent No. 1, who filed the application under Section 319 Cr.P.C., argued that the appellants should be summoned. This was based on their testimony as a witness (PW-1), where they reiterated allegations against the appellants, claiming they played an active role in the commission of the alleged offense.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the principles governing the exercise of power under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

cases.case_name: Sukhpal Singh Khaira v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the refreshed guidelines that a competent court must follow while exercising power under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain a discernible binding legal rule; it only directs the Trial Court to follow the dictum of previously decided cases.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the evidence on record was insufficient to summon most of the appellants, agreeing with the Trial Court's initial assessment that the deposition of Respondent No. 1 and other material did not establish their commission of an offense. However, the court differentiated the case of Appellant No. 1, concluding that the evidence against him alone was sufficient to meet the high threshold required to proceed against him as an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
legal_tests_applied: The extraordinary power vested under section 319 Cr.P.C ought to be exercised only if the evidence adduced on record strongly indicates the possible involvement of the person(s) aimed to be prosecuted.
why_appellant_lost: The appeal failed with respect to Appellant No. 1 because the court, after applying the legal standard, determined that the evidence against him was sufficient to proceed against him as an additional accused in the trial.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in having Appellant No. 1 summoned because the court was satisfied that the evidence against him met the high threshold of strongly indicating his possible involvement in the offense, thereby justifying the exercise of the extraordinary power under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
policy_considerations: While acknowledging the grave and heinous nature of the alleged offence and the need for justice ('The long arms of law must find out whether any person is guilty of abetting or taking away the precious life of a young girl'), the court emphasized that this objective is constrained by the strict legal requirement of evidentiary sufficiency, stating, 'However, the only issue that falls for our consideration is whether there is sufficient evidence against the Appellants to summon them as additional accused?'
